draft.title: The division of law-making powers
card: Exclusive
a power only the Commonwealth parliament may use. The states cannot make laws on it. Examples are customs and excise duties, and the power to coin money.
Concurrent
a power both the Commonwealth and the states may use. Examples are taxation (apart from customs and excise), marriage and trade.
Residual
a power the Constitution does not give to the Commonwealth, so it stays with the states. Examples are criminal law, education and public transport.
If a state law and a Commonwealth law clash on a concurrent power, the Commonwealth law wins. The state law is invalid to the extent of the clash.
draft.remember: Exclusive is Commonwealth only, concurrent is shared, residual is left to the states.

a.q: The Constitution does not give the Commonwealth power over a topic, so only the states make laws on it. What kind of power is this?
opts: A residual power
An exclusive power
A concurrent power
A delegated power
a.why: Powers left with the states because the Constitution does not give them to the Commonwealth are residual powers. An exclusive power is the reverse: only the Commonwealth may use it.
a.clue: Think about who is left with the power.

b.q: Both Victoria and the Commonwealth have passed laws on a shared topic, and the laws clash. Which statement is correct?
opts: The topic is concurrent, so the Commonwealth law prevails
The topic is exclusive, so the Commonwealth law prevails
The topic is concurrent, so the Victorian law prevails
The topic is residual, so the Commonwealth law prevails
b.why: Both parliaments can only make valid laws on the same topic if the power is concurrent. Where they clash, the Commonwealth law wins and the state law is invalid to the extent of the clash. An exclusive power would not allow a Victorian law at all.
b.clue: Which kind of power can both parliaments use?

b.best: The topic is concurrent, so the Commonwealth law prevails
